summary: Jesus tells His disciples that they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world, and calls them to let their good works be seen.
key_insight: Jesus says this to people He has just warned will be reviled and persecuted. The pressure would be to hide. Instead He says the light must be seen, and the result will be glory for their Father, not for them.
story: Jesus had just told His disciples they would be persecuted for His sake. Now He told them what they were in the world. “You are the salt of the earth,” He said. But if salt loses its flavor, nothing can make it salty again. It is good for nothing except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot.

“You are the light of the world. A city that is set on a hill cannot be hidden.” No one lights a lamp and then puts it under a basket. They set it on a lampstand, where it gives light to everyone in the house.
“Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven.”

scene.label: Salt
scene.text: Salt preserved fish and meat, seasoned food, and was added to every grain offering (Leviticus 2:13). Fish from the Sea of Galilee was salted and shipped across the region; Magdala, on the lake shore, was probably the town the Greeks called Taricheae, a name drawn from salted fish.

scene.label: Salt that loses its flavor
scene.text: Pure salt cannot lose its saltiness. But much of the salt used in Israel was gathered from the marshes and cliffs by the Dead Sea, mixed with other minerals. The usual explanation is that damp leached the true salt away, leaving a tasteless crust fit only for the path.

scene.label: A lamp and a basket
scene.text: A house lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick. The basket was a grain measure holding about two gallons; set over a lamp, it would hide the flame and soon put it out. Most village homes had one main room, so a single lamp on a stand lit the whole house.

scene.label: A light to the nations
scene.text: God had called His Servant to be “a light to the Gentiles” (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6), and the prophets pictured Jerusalem raised high with the nations streaming to it (Isaiah 2:2–3). Jesus speaks of His disciples in the same terms.

witnesses.matthew: Matthew alone keeps these sayings together at this point, right after the blessing on the persecuted. Mark and Luke record the salt and lamp sayings in other settings (Mark 4:21; 9:50; Luke 14:34–35), which suggests Jesus used these pictures more than once. Here “your Father in heaven” appears for the first of many times in the sermon.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the One who decides what His followers are. He gives a small band of ordinary Galileans the calling God gave Israel: to be salt for the earth and light for the world.
seeing.living: Salt works by contact and light by being seen. Do not withdraw from the people around you or hide your faith to stay safe, and let your good works be visible so that God, not you, receives the praise.
seeing.ponder: Where are you tempted to put your light under a basket, and whose praise are you seeking when it does shine?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus calls His people salt and light, to be seen for the Father’s glory.
outline: A light that cannot be hidden (14–15)
Good works that glorify the Father (16)
preaching.watch_for: Twice Jesus says “You are” (vv. 13, 14) before He gives a single command (v. 16). The command asks the disciples only to be what He has already said they are.
